units.t: How to Argue Well.
Part one. What a good argument needs.
Think about the last argument you had that went nowhere.
Maybe it was about politics at a family barbecue, or whose turn it was to do the dishes, or something a friend posted online.
Chances are, at some point, it stopped being about the question and started being about something else.
This lesson is about how that happens, and how to steer it back.
People have been cataloguing bad arguments for a very long time.
More than two thousand three hundred years ago, Aristotle wrote a short work usually known as On Sophistical Refutations.
In it, he listed thirteen ways an argument can look convincing while actually being faulty.
The sophists were paid teachers of persuasion in ancient Greece, and Aristotle thought many of them cared more about winning than about the truth.
Two thousand years later, the German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer came at it from the other side, with his tongue firmly in his cheek.
Around 1830, he wrote a short, sharp essay that was only published after his death.
It's usually translated as The Art of Being Right.
It lists thirty-eight dirty tricks for winning an argument, whether you're right or not.
Exaggerate your opponent's claim.
Make them angry.
If you're losing, change the subject.
Reading it today feels a lot like reading a comment section.
So what exactly is a fallacy?
In plain English, it's a mistake in reasoning that can make a weak argument sound strong.
It helps to separate two parts of any argument.
There are the reasons, which philosophers call premises.
And there's the conclusion, the thing the reasons are meant to support.
An argument can go wrong because the reasons are false.
Or it can go wrong because, even if the reasons were true, they wouldn't actually support the conclusion.
Most fallacies are the second kind.
The link between the reasons and the conclusion is broken, but it doesn't feel broken.
Philosophers split fallacies into two families, formal and informal.
Formal fallacies are errors in the bare structure of an argument, the kind you'd meet in a logic textbook.
Informal fallacies depend on the content and the context.
They're the ones you meet at work, at home and in the news, and they're what this lesson is about.
Here's something encouraging before we start.
Humans are often poor reasoners on our own, but surprisingly good reasoners together.
There's a famous logic puzzle called the Wason selection task, which only about one in ten people solve when they try it alone.
In a 1998 study, the psychologists David Moshman and Molly Geil gave the same puzzle to small groups who talked it through.
About three quarters of the groups got it right.
And it wasn't simply that one clever person told everyone else the answer.
The groups argued their way there, testing each other's reasons.
The French cognitive scientists Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber have built a whole theory on findings like this.
They suggest that human reasoning may have evolved mainly for arguing, for giving reasons to other people and weighing up theirs.
We're lazy about checking our own arguments, but sharp at spotting the flaws in someone else's.
That's why arguing well matters.
Done properly, a disagreement is one of the best tools we have for getting closer to the truth.
Done badly, it's just noise, and hurt feelings.
Over the next three parts, we'll meet twelve common fallacies, in three groups of four.
First, fallacies that attack the wrong target.
Then fallacies that rig the choices.
Then fallacies built on shaky evidence.
For each one, you'll hear what it sounds like, why it's tempting, and a calm way to answer it.
In the final part, we'll look at how to disagree without starting a fight, including one mistake that people who know all about fallacies make all the time.
If you're driving, there's nothing to write down or remember perfectly.
Just listen along, and notice which ones sound familiar.
Part two. Attacking the wrong target.
Our first group of fallacies share one feature.
Instead of dealing with the argument that was actually made, they aim somewhere else.
Fallacy number one is the straw man.
This is when you swap someone's real position for a weaker, sillier version, then knock that down instead.
The name comes from the idea of fighting a scarecrow rather than a real opponent.
It's much easier to win.
Here's an everyday example.
One parent says, I think the kids should have a bit less screen time on school nights.
The other replies, so you want to ban all technology and send them back to the Stone Age?
Nobody said that.
But now the first parent has to defend a position they never held.
The straw man is tempting because we often hear other people's views through our own frustration.
We remember the most extreme version of what they said, or what someone else on their side once said.
A good response is to calmly restate your actual point.
Try something like, that's not quite what I'm saying.
I'm saying one hour less on school nights.
Can we talk about that?
Fallacy number two is the ad hominem.
That's Latin for to the person.
It means attacking the person making an argument, instead of the argument itself.
Well, you would say that, you're a public servant.
What would you know, you've never run a business.
He can't be right about the budget, have you seen the state of his car?
Here's the key point.
Who someone is doesn't tell you whether their argument holds up.
A good argument from a person you dislike is still a good argument.
And a bad argument from your favourite person is still a bad one.
There's an important exception.
Sometimes a person's character or interests really are relevant.
Think of a witness in court, or a financial adviser recommending a product that pays them commission.
If you're relying on their word, it's fair to ask about their honesty and their incentives.
The fallacy is using the person to dismiss an argument whose reasons you could check for yourself.
A calm response is to steer back to those reasons.
Try, fair enough, but set me aside for a second.
What's wrong with the argument itself?
Fallacy number three is whataboutism.
Its older name is tu quoque, which is Latin for you too.
It means answering a criticism by pointing to someone else's bad behaviour, often the critic's own.
You tell a mate he shouldn't drive home after four beers, and he says, what about you, you drove after a few last month.
The tactic is strongly associated with the Cold War.
Critics have used the word to describe how Soviet officials answered criticism of their own record by pointing to problems in the West.
The trouble is that two wrongs don't make a right, as your nan probably told you.
Your mate's point about you might be fair.
You might even be a hypocrite.
That still doesn't make his drink driving safe.
Both things can be true at once.
A good reply accepts the hit and then returns to the point.
You're right, I shouldn't have done that either.
Let's both leave the car here tonight.
Fallacy number four is the red herring.
That's bringing up something irrelevant to pull attention away from the real question.
The name is usually linked to the idea of dragging a strong-smelling smoked fish across a trail to throw hunting dogs off the scent.
Word historians think the English journalist William Cobbett popularised the phrase in 1807, with a story that was probably made up.
Red herrings are everywhere in public life.
A company is asked why its prices went up, and the spokesperson talks about how many local jobs it creates.
A politician is asked about a broken promise and answers with a story about the other side's mistakes.
At home, it sounds like, why didn't you pay the phone bill, followed by, well, you never take the bins out.
The bins may be a genuine grievance.
But they're not the phone bill.
The best response is to name the topic, not the tactic.
Saying, that's a red herring, can sound like an accusation.
Instead, try, that might be worth talking about too.
Can we sort out the phone bill first?
Then come back to the bins.
Often people throw in red herrings not out of cunning but because they feel cornered.
Leaving them a dignified path back to the main topic helps.
Notice what these four have in common.
The straw man attacks a position nobody holds.
The ad hominem attacks the person.
Whataboutism attacks the critic.
And the red herring attacks a different topic altogether.
Whenever you feel an argument drifting, ask yourself one quiet question.
Are we still talking about the thing we started talking about?
Part three. Rigging the choices.
The second group of fallacies doesn't dodge the argument.
Instead, it quietly limits what's on the table, so that one conclusion seems forced.
Fallacy number five is the false dilemma, sometimes called a false choice, or black and white thinking.
It presents two options as if they're the only possibilities, when there are others.
Either we renovate the whole kitchen or we'll never sell this house.
Either you're with me on this or you're against me.
If you don't love your job, you should quit.
False dilemmas are tempting because they make decisions feel simple and urgent.
They're also a favourite of salespeople.
You can take the premium plan, or keep putting your family at risk.
Those are rarely the only two choices.
To answer a false dilemma, you don't need to argue hard for the other option.
Just widen the view.
Try, are those really the only two options?
What about a new benchtop and a fresh coat of paint?
Most real problems have a middle path, a third option, or a way to test things before fully committing.
Fallacy number six is the slippery slope.
It's the claim that one small step will inevitably set off a chain of events ending in disaster.
If we let the kids have dessert on a Tuesday, next they'll want it every night, and before you know it they'll be living on lollies.
If we allow one more cafe on the main street, the whole town will turn into a food court.
Here's where it gets interesting.
Not every slippery slope argument is a fallacy.
Some chains of events really do happen.
The question is whether each step in the chain is actually likely.
The fallacy is treating the slide as inevitable, without giving reasons for each link.
A calm response is to ask about those links.
Okay, walk me through it.
Why would dessert on one Tuesday lead to dessert every night?
Is there a point where we could just stop?
Often the chain turns out to have plenty of sensible places to stop.
Fallacy number seven is the loaded question.
That's a question with an assumption built into it, so that any direct answer seems to admit the assumption.
The textbook example is, have you stopped cheating at cards?
Answer yes, and you admit you used to cheat.
Answer no, and it sounds even worse.
Everyday versions are sneakier.
Why are you always so defensive?
Are you still wasting money on that gym you never go to?
How much longer are you going to ignore the problem?
Loaded questions work because questions feel innocent.
We're trained from childhood to answer them.
The trick is to answer the assumption, not the question.
Try, I don't agree that I'm always defensive.
Can you tell me what I did just now that felt that way?
That turns a trap into a real conversation.
Fallacy number eight is the middle ground, sometimes called the argument to moderation.
It's assuming the truth must lie halfway between two positions.
One engineer says a bridge is safe.
Another says it's about to collapse.
So the truth must be that it's half safe.
That's obviously silly with a bridge.
But we fall for it all the time with opinions, because splitting the difference feels fair and reasonable.
Compromise is often a great way to make a decision.
If you want to spend $400 on a new couch and your partner wants to spend $2,000, meeting somewhere in between might be exactly right.
That's a negotiation about preferences, and there's no single correct answer.
But when the disagreement is about facts, the midpoint has no special claim to truth.
If one person says water boils at one hundred degrees at sea level, and another insists it's fifty, the answer isn't seventy-five.
So a good response is to separate matters of taste from matters of fact.
Try, I'm happy to meet you halfway on how we do this.
But on whether it's true, let's look it up together.
That keeps the friendliness of compromise, without pretending that facts can be negotiated.
So that's the second group.
The false dilemma hides the other options.
The slippery slope hides the places you could stop.
The loaded question hides an assumption.
And the middle ground hides the difference between a fair deal and a true fact.
In each case, the answer is to gently reveal what's been hidden, without trying to score points.
Part four. Shaky evidence, shaky links.
Our third group of fallacies is about evidence.
These are the mistakes that turn a story, a coincidence or a label into something that feels like proof.
Fallacy number nine is the hasty generalisation.
That's drawing a broad conclusion from too few examples.
My grandad smoked a pack a day and lived to ninety-five, so smoking can't be that bad.
I went to that cafe once and the coffee was cold, so it's a terrible cafe.
My neighbour's electric car nearly ran flat on a country road, so they're useless for road trips.
The pull here is that one vivid story feels more real than a mountain of statistics.
We're built to learn from stories.
Your grandad was a real person you loved.
A table of health figures is not.
But one case, however vivid, can't tell you what usually happens.
For every grandad who smoked into his nineties, there were many who never got the chance.
A gentle response is to take the story seriously, then ask about the bigger picture.
That's a great innings.
I wonder how common that is, though.
Do we know what happens to most smokers?
That honours the person's experience, without letting one story stand in for the evidence.
Fallacy number ten has a Latin name, post hoc, ergo propter hoc.
It means after this, therefore because of this.
It's assuming that because one thing happened after another, the first must have caused the second.
I wore my lucky socks and my team won.
I started taking a vitamin and my cold cleared up in a week.
The new manager started in March, and sales went up in April.
Our brains are cause-finding machines, and usually that's useful.
If you eat an unfamiliar berry and feel sick an hour later, it's smart to avoid that berry.
But things often happen one after another by pure coincidence.
Most colds clear up in about a week anyway.
Sales might have risen because of the season, or the economy, or a competitor closing down.
A close cousin is confusing correlation with causation.
Ice cream sales and drownings both rise at the same time of year.
Ice cream doesn't cause drowning.
Hot weather drives both.
When someone tells you one thing caused another, a good calm question is, what else could explain that?
Or, what would have happened anyway?
Fallacy number eleven is the appeal to nature.
It's the assumption that natural means good or safe, and unnatural means bad.
It's all natural, so it can't hurt you.
That's not natural, so it must be wrong.
Australians should be especially immune to this one, because plenty of our most natural things are deadly.
The venom of the eastern brown snake is completely natural.
So is the box jellyfish.
So is the gympie-gympie, a rainforest stinging tree whose sting can hurt for weeks.
On the other side, plenty of very unnatural things are extremely good for us, from glasses to clean tap water to vaccines.
Natural is also a slippery word.
Is bread natural?
It doesn't grow on trees.
What about a herbal supplement made in a factory and sold in a plastic bottle?
When someone leans hard on the word natural, a useful response is to ask about the thing itself, not the label.
Try, natural sounds nice, but is it safe, and does it actually work?
What's the evidence?
Fallacy number twelve has a wonderful name.
It's the no true Scotsman.
The British philosopher Antony Flew described it in the 1970s with a little story, which goes roughly like this in paraphrase.
A Scotsman reads in the paper about a terrible crime committed by an Englishman, and says, no Scotsman would do such a thing.
The next day, he reads about an even worse crime, committed by a Scotsman.
Instead of changing his mind, he says, well, no true Scotsman would do such a thing.
The fallacy is protecting a claim from any evidence against it by quietly redefining the group.
You'll hear local versions all the time.
No true Aussie dislikes Vegemite.
And when you meet an Aussie who can't stand the stuff, well, they're not a real Aussie.
No real fan leaves before the final siren.
Every counterexample is simply defined away, so the claim can never be shown to be wrong.
That's why it's worth answering with one simple question.
What would it take to change your mind?
If the honest answer is nothing at all, then the claim isn't really about the world anymore.
It's about how we've chosen to use a word.
A close relative is moving the goalposts.
That's when, every time someone meets a standard of evidence, a new and higher standard appears.
Across these four, the common thread is this.
Stories, sequences, labels and definitions can all feel like evidence without actually being evidence.
The calm questions to reach for are these.
How typical is that?
What else could explain it?
What's the actual evidence?
And what would change your mind?
Part five. Disagreeing without a fight.
You now know twelve fallacies.
So here's the most important warning in the whole lesson.
Knowing the names of fallacies can make you a worse arguer, not a better one.
Imagine someone makes a reasonable point in a clumsy way, and you jump in with, that's an ad hominem, or, that's a slippery slope.
Even if you're technically right, you've just told them they're foolish.
They'll dig in.
And there's a deeper problem.
An argument with a fallacy in it can still have a true conclusion.
Your friend might say the new intersection is dangerous because the engineer who designed it is an idiot.
That's an ad hominem.
But the intersection might still be dangerous.
Rejecting a conclusion just because someone argued for it badly is itself a mistake.
It even has a name.
The fallacy fallacy.
So the goal isn't to catch people out.
It's to get closer to the truth together, and keep the relationship in one piece.
Here are some tools that help.
The first comes from the American philosopher Daniel Dennett.
In his 2013 book Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking, he described what he called Rapoport's rules, named after the mathematician and game theorist Anatol Rapoport.
Here they are, in paraphrase.
First, restate the other person's position so clearly, vividly and fairly that they say, thanks, I wish I'd thought of putting it that way.
Second, list any points where you agree, especially ones that aren't widely shared.
Third, mention anything you've learned from them.
Only then, fourth, are you allowed to say a single word of criticism.
It sounds almost too polite.
But think about what it does.
By the time you disagree, the other person knows you've actually understood them, so they're far more likely to listen.
It's also the exact opposite of the straw man.
People sometimes call this steelmanning.
You argue against the strongest version of someone's view, rather than the weakest.
The second tool is a question.
How would that actually work?
In 2013, a team led by the cognitive scientist Philip Fernbach worked with Americans who held strong opinions on political issues.
They asked them to explain, step by step, how their preferred policy would actually work.
Not why they supported it.
Just how it would work.
After trying, most people realised they understood the issue less well than they'd thought, and their views became less extreme.
Interestingly, asking people to list their reasons for their view didn't have the same effect.
Listing reasons tends to harden a position.
Explaining the mechanics tends to soften it.
This builds on an earlier finding called the illusion of explanatory depth.
The researchers Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil found that people believe they understand everyday things, like zips, flushing toilets and locks, far better than they really do.
Ask them to explain one step by step, and their confidence drains away.
You can use this kindly in any disagreement.
Instead of saying, you're wrong, try, that's interesting, how would that work in practice?
And ask it of yourself, too.
The third tool is to aim high on what the essayist Paul Graham called the hierarchy of disagreement.
In a 2008 essay, he ranked ways of disagreeing from worst to best.
At the bottom is name-calling.
Then attacking the person.
Then responding to their tone rather than their content.
Then simple contradiction, just stating the opposite.
Higher up comes counterargument, giving reasons for a different view.
Then refutation, showing exactly where their argument goes wrong.
And at the very top, refuting their central point, not some side issue.
Most arguments that go badly never climb past the middle.
It's also worth letting go of one popular idea.
You may have heard of the backfire effect.
That's the claim that correcting people with facts makes them cling even harder to their false belief.
It came from a well-known study published in 2010.
But when the political scientists Thomas Wood and Ethan Porter tested it with more than ten thousand people, across dozens of issues, they found it was rare.
Most people shifted at least a little towards the facts.
So facts do help.
They just work better when they're offered with respect, and when the other person doesn't have to lose face to accept them.
That leads to a final practical point.
Give people a way to change their mind with dignity.
Nobody likes to admit defeat in front of an audience.
Try saying things like, I used to think that too.
Or, I can see why that seems right.
Or, let's both look it up.
Sometimes the best move is to let an argument rest and come back to it tomorrow, when nobody has to win in front of anyone.
And be ready to change your own mind.
The whole point of spotting fallacies is to reason better, and that includes your own reasoning.
If you catch yourself building a straw man, or reaching for a what about you, just say so.
It's disarming, and it's honest.
So here are the key takeaways.
Most fallacies either attack the wrong target, rig the choices, or pass off stories and coincidences as evidence.
Each can be answered with a calm question instead of an accusation.
A badly argued point can still be true, so understand the strongest version of the other view before you criticise it.
And arguing well isn't about winning, it's about getting closer to the truth together.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What's the name for swapping someone's real position for a weaker version and attacking that instead?
Answer. The straw man.
Question two. What does post hoc, ergo propter hoc mean?
Answer. After this, therefore because of this. Assuming that what came first caused what came next.
Question three. What's the fallacy fallacy?
Answer. Rejecting a conclusion just because someone argued for it badly. A poorly argued point can still be true.
That's the end of How to Argue Well. Go well, and argue kindly.
